name: Uradhi, Yadhaykenu dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 1983. 'Uradhi'. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, Vol. 3, 306-428. Canberra: ANU Press / Amsterdam: John Benjamins. (ANU Open Research digitisation hdl:1885/114846)
catalog_locator: p. 322, section 2.3 'Stress'; vowel-length distribution p. 318 (excerpt); dialect identity pp. 307-309 (excerpt)
catalog_quote: 2.3 STRESS The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/ 'person' /íku/ 'bandicoot' /ín̪t̪inu/ 'story-place of brown snake' /t̪úɣuβa/ 'cigarette' /umúɣan̪u/ 'nose' /ukúmala/ 'sweet potato' /ayparúmpiwa/ 'sparrowhawk' (ii) In the case of words containing long vowels, it is always the long vowels that receive primary stress, regardless of their position in the word. (Note that it is possible to have a word that contains two primary stresses.) The following examples (again from the Atampaya dialect) are chosen to illustrate this: /it̪í:na/ 'thigh' /amá:ka/ 'message stick' /t̪á:rá:namu/ 'reef-GEN'
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Long vowels always carry primary stress wherever they are (a word with two long vowels has two primary stresses); in words with only short vowels primary stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable, which means the initial syllable in words of one to three syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the section only speaks of primary stress and notes that a word may have two primary stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the long-vowel override. Note the earlier, independent description of the Uradhi-proper dialect by Hale (1976, Sutton ed.), seen only in search snippets: 'Uradhi and Umbindharnu stress the first vowel after a consonant (with the possible exception that initial long vowels are stressed..)', which would put stress on the second syllable of vowel-initial words, unlike Crowley's /áma/.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; the rules are stated for 'the Uradhi dialects' jointly (Crowley §1.1 names them as Atampaya, Angkamuthi and Yadhaykenu), but every example is from Atampaya; no Yadhaykenu-specific examples or statement. The three dialects were recorded at Cowal Creek (Injinoo) in a salvage study.
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 1983 describes 'the Uradhi dialects' as one language: Atampaya (atam1239), Angkamuthi (angg1238) and Yadhaykenu (yadh1237), all recorded at Cowal Creek/Injinoo. The stress section is stated for all three dialects jointly but illustrated only with Atampaya forms; the same page already serves as the catalog's source for atam1239 (and the retired urad1239). Hale's 'Uradhi' (1964, 1976) is the distinct Uradhi-proper dialect (Glottolog places it in the same Uradhic group), not Yadhaykenu. Ray 1907's 'Yaraikana' = Yadhaykenu.

new_statements.quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss or other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it, is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. Even in Uraði, the prevailing tendency has been toward initial loss, although *C1 is sometimes positively reflected in that language.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (Crowley 1983 p. 322) records a weight-sensitive rule with primary stress on the antepenult, i.e. word-initial in words of up to three short-vowel syllables (/áma/ 'person'), and long vowels always stressed. Hale 1964 instead places Northern Paman primary stress on the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, as a phonetic feature, with no role for vowel length (he has long *V1 shortened in all Northern Paman languages). For a Uradhi dialect that keeps the initial vowel, that puts stress on the post-consonantal (second) vowel, e.g. amá rather than Crowley's áma, which matches the Hale 1976a windows already logged ('Uradhi and Umbindharnu stress the first vowel after a consonant'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A diachronic, group-level statement only: in the Northern Paman languages primary stress (called 'a strictly phonetic feature') shifted from the first to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, and this shift is held partly responsible for the loss of initial consonants and vowels. Uradhi and its sister dialects (which include Ray's Yaraikana = Yadhaykenu, said on p. 252 to share about 83% of basic vocabulary with Hale's Uradhi) are the exception to initial loss: *C1 is sometimes kept (p. 256) and short *V1 'was neither lost nor metathesized' (p. 260). No synchronic stress rule for Uradhi or Yadhaykenu is stated anywhere in the paper; there is no phonology or stress section for any individual language, no vowel-length condition, and no example marked for stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none for stress as such; Uradhi and its sister dialects are named as the exception to initial-consonant loss (*C1 sometimes reflected, p. 256) and to loss of short *V1 (p. 260)
new_statements.identity_note: Hale's 'Uradhi' (/uraði/) is Uradhi proper: the informant learned it from his father from McDonnell on the Skardon River (p. 252). Hale says it is similar to Ray's Yaraikana (= Yadhaykenu), sharing some 83% of basic vocabulary, and that Yaraikana, Bandji, Gudang, Ngamiti, Wo:tati, Yumakundyi and Mu:tyati are 'probably dialects of a single language' with Uradhi. Yadhaykenu itself was not sampled; the stress remark on p. 256 is about the Northern Paman group as a whole ('Paman stems').

readall_conflicts: Hale 1964 (p. 256) says Northern Paman primary stress moved from the initial to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem and treats stress as a purely phonetic feature with no length condition; Crowley 1983 (p. 322, the catalog's source) gives the Uradhi dialects antepenultimate (initial in short words) primary stress in all-short-vowel words, e.g. /áma/ 'person', with long vowels always taking primary stress. On a word that keeps its initial vowel these predict different syllables (amá vs áma). Hale's statement is group-level and diachronic, and is consistent with the second-hand Hale 1976a windows already in 'stress the first vowel after a consonant', for Uradhi proper). So the disagreement is really Hale (1964, 1976a: Uradhi proper, informant from the Skardon River) versus Crowley (1983: Atampaya examples, rule stated for all three dialects including Yadhaykenu); no source gives Yadhaykenu-specific stressed examples.

sources.note: p.322 §2.3 Stress: rules 'throughout the Uradhi dialects' (Atampaya, Angkamuthi, Yadhaykenu) are 'fairly uniform': primary stress on the antepenultimate syllable of words containing only short vowels (initial in words of <=3 syllables); long vowels always receive primary stress regardless of position, so a word may carry two primary stresses. All examples Atampaya (/áma/, /íku/, /ukúmala/, /ayparúmpiwa/; /it̪í:na/, /amá:ka/, /t̪á:rá:namu/). Nothing on secondary stress.
